flagship.name: UCT Foundations
flagship.blurb: The start-here spine: fourteen modules that install the complete UCT operating loop — regime, breadth/RS confirmation, scan, setup, size, manage, review — taught risk-first, one concept per lesson, and finishing with a defended personal playbook. Videos come from the library's most course-shaped teaching; every proprietary UCT layer (regime engine, exposure ladder, sizing table, journal system) is a named gap recording.

modules.module_label: Module 1 — The Game: Probabilities, Regimes, and Your First Exposure Call
modules.purpose: Install the probabilistic frame and the UCT operating loop, and ship a real usable skill in the first sitting (read the regime dial, write an exposure plan) to beat the week-1-2 dropout window. Guardrail stated in this module: until Module 11 (setup grading) a member cannot yet grade a setup — treat every candidate as B-grade max and trade pilot size (or paper) until Module 5's risk math is cleared.

lessons.why: Clearest lesson in the library on why edges pay and predictions don't — verified at chapter t=2:36 (0:02:36), the exact casino-math line: "90% win-rate at 0.1:1 reward loses money; 30% win-rate at 3:1..." — the opener the dossier mandates. Whole 47-minute video stays on this single thread (AMD/Snowflake/Snap/Lululemon examples all illustrate the same math), so it needs no timestamp pointer.

lessons.title: The Whole Game in One Sitting: Trade Types, Regime Reading, and Invalidation
lessons.why: The batch's most complete single swing-trading workshop — verified via its own chapter list: scalp/day/swing trade-type distinctions (0:00, 4:02), invalidation-spot mechanics (8:20, 73:20 "identify invalidation zones, map targets 2x risk"), risk-on-vs-range regime reading (45:00 — the direct throughline into this module's Regimes theme), and sector sympathy plays (50:00 XLF/XLI/solar). A full shallow-breadth first pass per the TraderLion funnel move, before any deep module begins.
lessons.chapter_note: Watch from 0:00 — trade-type distinctions (scalp/day/swing), 8:20 — invalidation-spot mechanics (identify invalidation zones, map targets 2x risk), and 45:00 — risk-on-vs-range regime reading; these three timestamps are verified against the video's own chapter list and are the segments confirmed to survive the AI-chapter-drift issue found elsewhere in this batch. The 8:20-40:00 stretch in between drifts into Module 13 options material and is out of scope for this lesson.

briefs.title: The UCT Operating Loop: Regime → Scan → Setup → Size → Manage → Review
briefs.placement: UCT Foundations (Flagship Course), Module 1 — The Game: Probabilities, Regimes, and Your First Exposure Call, Lesson 3 of 4 (after 'The Whole Game in One Sitting: Trade Types, Regime Reading, and Invalidation', before 'Early Win: Read Today's Regime Dial and Write Your First Max-Exposure Plan')
talking_points: The loop has seven stops in a fixed order — Regime, Breadth/RS Confirm, Scan, Setup, Size, Manage, Review — and each one gates the next; you cannot legally skip forward.
Regime first: check today's UCT Exposure Rating (0-150) and its GREEN/YELLOW/ORANGE state before opening a single chart — it decides how much of the rest of the loop you're even allowed to use today.

Breadth/RS confirm: do breadth and relative strength agree with the dial? (Module 4 teaches the five numbers) — this is its own explicit stop between Regime and Scan; nothing below it fires until breadth and RS agree with what the dial says.
Scan: the day's actionable names come from the firm's scan output — the loop exists to narrow the universe to only what already passed the regime check.

Setup: name the pattern from the 24-setup playbook's four families (Bases & Breakouts, Momentum & Trend, Gaps & Catalysts, Reversals & Reclaims) and the entry type — PREV DAY HIGH BREAK, PREV LOW RECLAIM, RED TO GREEN, or BASE BREAKOUT — before you touch a share.
Size: Account Risk % = Position Size % x Stop Distance %, capped at 2% and preferring under 1%, then scaled down further by the regime state you checked in step one.
Manage: execute the plan you wrote at entry, then manage it — not improvising. Review: every closed trade re-enters the loop as data — this is where the loop closes, not ends.
The one-sentence self-test for 'did I run the loop': for the trade you're about to take, can you name exactly which of the seven steps you're on right now?
briefs.open_with: You've just found a chart you love — a tight base, a clean breakout candle. Before you place the order, one question kills more accounts than any bad setup ever will: what's today's regime? If you can't answer that in one second, you've already skipped the first step of the loop — and the setup doesn't matter yet.
briefs.close_with: Takeaway: seven stops, fixed order, each one gates the next — Regime, Breadth/RS Confirm, Scan, Setup, Size, Manage, Review. You don't need to master any of them yet; you need the order in your head so nothing downstream — Module 3's regime engine, Module 5's risk math, Modules 6-9's setups — ever floats free of the sequence again. Next: the Early Win — read today's actual regime dial and write your first exposure plan.

briefs.title: Early Win: Read Today's Regime Dial and Write Your First Max-Exposure Plan
briefs.placement: UCT Foundations (Flagship Course), Module 1 — The Game: Probabilities, Regimes, and Your First Exposure Call, Lesson 4 of 4 (closing lesson of the module, after 'The UCT Operating Loop: Regime → Scan → Setup → Size → Manage → Review')
talking_points: Today's UCT Exposure Rating is a single number, 0-150, rebuilt fresh every morning — this is the first lesson where you read it as a trading input, not a dashboard curiosity.
Translate the number to a state: GREEN, YELLOW, or ORANGE — then pair it with a setup grade (A+, A, B...) to land on a rung of the exposure ladder.
The four rungs to memorize today: GREEN+A+ = 20-25% position size, YELLOW+A+ = 15%, ORANGE+A+ = 8%, and B-grade in ORANGE = skip entirely, full stop.
Worked example, live on-screen: pull up today's actual dial reading, name the state out loud, and size a hypothetical A+ setup using the ladder.
Write it down: the one-page Max-Exposure Plan worksheet — today's date, today's score, today's state, today's max size per rung, one sentence on what would flip your read by tomorrow.
The plan is disposable by design — it expires at tomorrow's open. The skill isn't the paper, it's the two-minute habit of checking regime before checking anything else.
Practice rep: fill out the worksheet against today's real market, not a simulation — this is the course's first genuine trading decision, made in week one.
Guardrail: until Module 11 you cannot grade a setup — treat every candidate as B-grade max, and trade pilot size (or paper) until you clear Module 5's risk math.
briefs.open_with: Most courses make you wait weeks to do something real. Not this one. Open the dashboard right now — you're going to read today's actual UCT Exposure number, and by the end of this lesson you'll have a written plan for exactly how big you're allowed to trade today. This is the whole game in miniature, on day one.
briefs.close_with: Takeaway: you now hold a real, dated exposure plan — not a concept, a decision — and that's the habit that repeats every trading morning for the rest of this course. Next: Module 2 — Chart Literacy, where you learn to actually read what's in front of you before you ever apply a rule to it.

briefs.title: The Four Stages of Any Stock, Then the Stage-2 Gate (8-Point Binary Checklist)
briefs.placement: UCT Foundations (Flagship Course), Module 3 — The Regime Engine: Stages, Market Direction, and the Exposure Model, Lesson 1 of 5 (opening lesson of the module, before 'The Trading-Environment Checklist: MA Slope, What's Working, and When to Sit Out')
talking_points: Part 1 — perception, no rules yet: one diagram, four stages — Stage 1 basing (flat, low volume), Stage 2 advancing (rising, above a rising average), Stage 3 topping (wide and loose), Stage 4 declining (below a falling average). Look at ten real charts and just NAME the stage — no buy/sell logic attached.
The cycle is one continuous wheel, not four separate patterns — a stock is always somewhere on it, and it keeps turning after Stage 4 back into Stage 1.
Micro-check between parts: cover the answer on a fresh chart and call the stage before flipping it over — this tests the gestalt, not a definition.
Part 2 — the gate: the Stage-2 Trend Template is 8 yes/no criteria, ALL eight required — fail even one and the stock is not eligible to trade, no exceptions.

Name the eight criteria as an on-screen checklist a member can pause and copy: price above both the 150-day and 200-day average; 150-day above 200-day; 200-day trending up at least a month; 50-day above the 150- and 200-day; price above the 50-day; price at least 25% above its 52-week low; price within 25% of its 52-week high; relative strength holding, not lagging the market.
This is a binary eligibility gate, not a grading rubric — it answers only 'is this stock in play,' and says nothing yet about entry, timing, or setup quality.
Worked example: run one real stock through all eight boxes live to a pass, then run one that fails on a single criterion to show 'fail one, skip the stock' has no soft landing.
Named exercise: pull 15 stocks from today's scan and run all eight boxes on each — 80% correct pass/fail calls required to clear the checkpoint.
briefs.open_with: Look at this chart for three seconds — where is it in its life cycle? Don't look for a setup, don't check an indicator. Just tell me: is this stock resting, climbing, topping, or falling? If you can't answer that before anything else, everything downstream — the regime engine, the scan, every setup in this course — is being applied to a stock you never actually looked at first.
briefs.close_with: Takeaway: every stock lives on one four-stage wheel, and Stage 2 has a hard, binary door — eight checks, all eight required, one failure locks it. You now have a mechanical first filter that needs zero judgment. Next: we take this exact lens off a single stock and put it on SPY, QQQ, and IWM — the market itself moves through the same four stages.

briefs.title: Inside the UCT Regime Model: The Inputs, the States, and What Flips Them
briefs.placement: UCT Foundations (Flagship Course), Module 3 — The Regime Engine: Stages, Market Direction, and the Exposure Model, Lesson 4 of 5 (after 'Confirming a Market Bottom: Follow-Through Days, Distribution Days, and the MA-Reclaim Checklist', before 'The Exposure Ladder: Position Count, Size, and New-Buy Rights by Regime State')
talking_points: This is the system's identity lesson: the UCT Exposure Rating is not a mood — it's a computed score, 0-150, rebuilt fresh every morning from real market-breadth inputs.
The three named states — GREEN, YELLOW, ORANGE — are bands on that one score, not separate models; it's the same raw number you first read in Module 1's Early Win.

Name the input family the score is built from — breadth conditions like advance/decline, % of stocks above key moving averages, and new highs vs new lows — the same market-internal signals Module 4 will teach you to read yourself.
The scoring stacks a base reading plus bonus tiers when multiple conditions confirm together, up to a 150 ceiling — that's why the number moves in jumps, not a smooth drift.
What actually flips a state: walk one real historical transition where the breadth inputs crossed a threshold and the color changed, showing the score before and after.
The state is a permission system, not a prediction — GREEN doesn't mean 'the market goes up,' it means 'more of your playbook is authorized today.' Test that distinction explicitly before moving on.
Guess-before-you-check: given yesterday's breadth numbers with the state covered, call GREEN/YELLOW/ORANGE yourself, then reveal the actual reading.
Named exercise: log the regime state for the last 10 trading days from the dashboard's own history and mark the day it changed — the raw material for the module's closing drill.
briefs.open_with: Every member sees a number on this dashboard every morning — 0 to 150 — and most of them have never once been told where it comes from. Today that changes: you're going to see, input by input, exactly what builds the UCT Exposure Rating and exactly what has to happen in the market for that number to move from one color to another.
briefs.close_with: Takeaway: the regime score isn't a black box — it's built from breadth you can eventually check yourself, and its whole job is to tell you what you're permitted to do, not what will happen next. Next: the exposure ladder — what each of these regime states actually permits you to do.

briefs.title: The Exposure Ladder: What Each Regime State Permits
briefs.placement: UCT Foundations (Flagship Course), Module 3 — The Regime Engine: Stages, Market Direction, and the Exposure Model, Lesson 5 of 5 (closing lesson of the module, after 'Inside the UCT Regime Engine: GREEN/YELLOW/ORANGE States, the 0-150 Exposure Score, and What Flips Them')
talking_points: This lesson answers one question only: given today's state, what are you actually allowed to do — not what to look for, that's a later module's job.
The ladder in numbers, memorized: GREEN + A+ setup = 20-25% position size; YELLOW + A+ = 15%; ORANGE + A+ = 8%; B-grade setup in ORANGE = skip, no trade.
This is the same ladder from Module 1's Early Win — the difference now is you know WHY those numbers exist, tied directly to the regime engine you just opened up.
New-buy rights change by state, not just size — at ORANGE, depending on setup grade, you can lose the right to open new names at all, not just shrink them.
Position count is regime-gated too — the number of names you're permitted to hold open scales down in the same direction as size.
Worked example: take one A+ setup and size it three different ways, once per state, side by side — the same chart producing three different, correct answers depending only on regime.
The ladder is a ceiling, never a floor — nothing here tells you to take the max; it tells you the most you're permitted, full stop.
Named exercise: given 5 setup grades across 5 mixed regime states, fill in the permitted size for each — 80% correct required to clear.
Guardrail: until Module 11 you cannot grade a setup — treat every candidate as B-grade max, and trade pilot size (or paper) until you clear Module 5's risk math.
briefs.open_with: Same A+ setup, same chart, same stop — but here's the catch: the correct position size for this exact trade is three different numbers depending on one thing you haven't checked yet. What's today's regime state? Until you answer that, 'how big do I buy this' has no correct answer at all.
briefs.close_with: Takeaway: the regime state doesn't just color a dashboard tile — it sets a hard ceiling on size, position count, and even whether new buys are permitted at all. You now hold the full authorization table this course has been building toward since Module 1. Next: Module 4 — Breadth, Relative Strength, and the Scan Engine, where the regime read you just learned to size against gets its own confirming layer.

briefs.title: Volume as the Witness: Confirmation as Its Own Verdict
briefs.placement: UCT Foundations (Flagship Course), Module 4 — Breadth, Relative Strength, and the Scan Engine, Lesson 4 of 5 (after 'Building the Morning Watchlist: 7 Custom Scanners and the Single-Screen Routine', before 'Your Daily Market-Health Scorecard: Five Numbers Before the Open')
talking_points: The question this lesson exists to teach, asked by itself: does this signal have a witness? Price can lie; volume is the only thing in the room that has to show up honestly.
Reframe: every setup lesson in Modules 6-9 mentions volume as a bullet point — this is the one lesson where volume is graded on its own, as a stand-alone skill, never folded into a pattern.
Confirmed vs unconfirmed, with real triggers: a PREV DAY HIGH BREAK on light volume is a different trade than the identical break on expanding volume — same price action, different verdict.

Bring in the firm's own scanner vocabulary as the concrete case: volume accumulation ratio (up-day volume vs down-day volume) and an N-week volume low ahead of a move — signals the firm already computes, now read as their own verdict.
The false-positive case: a breakout that looks clean on price alone but has no volume witness — walk one real chart where the pattern was right and the volume said no, and show what happened next.
The false-negative case: a quiet base with volume drying up for weeks — the N-week-low tell — that later explodes; volume was whispering the answer before price moved.
Guess-before-you-check: 8 charts, price pattern visible, volume panel covered — call 'witnessed' or 'not witnessed,' then reveal the volume.
Named exercise: pull 10 setups from today's scan candidates and grade each one's volume witness independently of its setup grade — two separate scores on paper, never one blended gut call.
briefs.open_with: Here's a breakout that looks perfect — clean base, tight pullback, textbook trigger candle. I'm going to cover the volume panel and ask you one question: would you buy it? Now I'll show you the volume — and notice your answer to 'is this a good setup' just changed without a single candle moving.
briefs.close_with: Takeaway: volume isn't a bullet point inside a setup lesson — it's an independent verdict you run on every signal, every time, before size ever enters the conversation. Next: you'll fold this witness-check into the five numbers on your daily market-health scorecard — the habit that closes out Module 4.

briefs.title: Your Daily Market-Health Scorecard: Five Numbers Before the Open (With the Morning Wire)
briefs.placement: UCT Foundations (Flagship Course), Module 4 — Breadth, Relative Strength, and the Scan Engine, Lesson 5 of 5 (closing lesson of the module, after 'Volume as the Witness: Confirmation as Its Own Verdict')
talking_points: The five numbers, named: % of stocks above the 50-day, the advance-decline line, new highs vs. new lows, your stock's comparative RS-line slope vs. SPY, and the UCT Exposure Rating (0-150)

Where each number physically lives in the product: Breadth Monitor tile, the RS panel, and the regime banner at the top of today's Morning Wire — this is not a hypothetical worksheet, it's a five-minute reading of a page that already exists
Reading the UCT Exposure Rating cold: 110+ is extreme-green, 90-109 green, 70-89 mild green, 50-69 amber caution, below 50 is red-tier — tie each band back to the regime states installed in Module 3
Worked example, live: pull today's actual Morning Wire and fill the five-number scorecard on camera, narrating each read as you go, including one number that disagrees with the other four

Confirmation vs. contradiction: what it means when breadth agrees with price (a healthy green tape) vs. when RS-line new highs arrive before price highs — the institutional-accumulation tell from Module 4's earlier lesson
The daily-cadence mechanic: 'today's Wire IS your Module 4 scorecard, filled in' — the live product becomes the spaced-repetition layer that keeps this skill from decaying after the course ends
The one-page worksheet: five labeled blanks, five named sources, filled in before every single open — not 'check the market,' a literal five-line form
The failure mode this kills: trading off one number in isolation (SPY green, so buy) while the other four are flashing a thin, unhealthy tape
briefs.open_with: Cold open: SPY is up 1% at the open and it looks like a green light to add exposure — except only 38% of stocks are above their 50-day and new lows are outpacing new highs. That's the 'green candle, red breadth' trap, and by the end of this lesson you'll never fall into it again because you'll have five numbers, not one, before you make any call.
briefs.close_with: Takeaway: five numbers, one worksheet, filled in from today's actual Wire before every open — breadth is the market's internal X-ray, and now you read it daily instead of guessing off the index candle. Next up: Module 5 — Risk Math, First Pass: R, Expectancy, and the 2% Ceiling, starting with 'Where the Stop Actually Goes: Thesis Invalidation, Not Comfort' — now that you can read the market's health, you learn where your risk begins before you learn how much of it to take.

briefs.title: Expectancy and Drawdown Arithmetic: Grade Your System With Your Own Numbers
briefs.placement: UCT Foundations (Flagship Course), Module 5 — Risk Math, First Pass: R, Expectancy, and the 2% Ceiling, Lesson 4 of 4 (closing lesson of the module, after 'Entries That Maximize R: Identify Your Invalidation Spot First')
talking_points: Quick distinction up front: the earlier 2R-minimum lesson filters ONE trade before entry; expectancy grades the WHOLE SYSTEM after the fact, using your closed trades — different question, different tool

The expectancy equation, worked three times on camera: (Win% × Avg Win R) − (Loss% × Avg Loss R) — a 45%-win-rate system averaging 2.5R on winners beats a 70%-win-rate system averaging 0.5R on winners
Where to pull YOUR real numbers: Journal → Analytics tab — win rate, average R, profit factor, computed from your own closed trades, never estimated or assumed
Worked example, live: hand-compute expectancy from a sample 20-trade run, then verify the hand math against the Journal's own Edge Score number
Drawdown arithmetic, the table stated plainly: minus-10% needs plus-11% to recover, minus-25% needs plus-33%, minus-50% needs plus-100% — the math gets worse, not linearly, as the hole deepens

Why this table is the actual justification for regime-off discipline: a big drawdown isn't just a bigger number, it's a mathematically harder climb — this is the arithmetic behind every ORANGE/RED sizing rule taught later
The exercise: pull your own last 20 closed trades right now, hand-compute win rate and average R, and compare your answer to what the Edge Score already shows you

The grading rule to end on: expectancy above zero means keep running the system as-is; expectancy at or below zero means stop and diagnose the specific broken sub-skill — never just 'try harder' or add more reps blind

Account-level de-risking triggers, stated as firm policy: at -5% account drawdown, cut size and tighten setup grade (B-grade candidates drop entirely); at -10% account drawdown, stand down to pilot size or paper only until a full review clears you to resume — this is the specific rule Module 11's regime-sizing table cross-references back to this lesson.
briefs.open_with: You just took two losses in a row and you're ready to abandon the system. But is the system actually broken, or are you inside a completely normal losing streak for a profitable edge? You cannot tell the difference by feel — you can only tell by doing this math, on your own numbers, right now.
briefs.close_with: Takeaway: expectancy is the only honest grade of a trading system, and drawdown arithmetic is the reason the whole regime-sizing ladder exists later in the course. Next up: 'The 24-Play Book: Four Families, and Primary vs. Add-On vs. Exit Plays' — you now know how to size a trade and grade a system; next you learn what's actually in the system you're grading.

briefs.title: The 24-Play Book: Four Families, and Primary vs. Add-On vs. Exit Plays
briefs.placement: UCT Foundations (Flagship Course), Module 6 — Setup Family I: Bases and Breakouts, Lesson 1 of 4 (opening lesson of the module, before 'The Breakout, End-to-End: Scan, Entry, Stop, and Position Sizing (Stair-Step Family)')
talking_points: The whole book at a glance: four families — Bases & Breakouts, Momentum & Trend, Gaps & Catalysts, Reversals & Reclaims — each family gets its own module (6 through 9), one flagship setup taught to full depth, the rest taught as named variants
Function tier one, PRIMARY entries — the plays that open a brand-new position: Flat Base Breakout, Cup & Handle, Episodic Pivot, Power Earnings Gap
Function tier two, ADD-ON/continuation plays — used to add to a winner you already hold, never to open a new trade: 20 EMA Pullback, EMA Crossback, Bull Flag

Function tier three, EXIT-side reads — plays that tell you to get out or tighten up, not to get in: a Parabolic Long as a topping tell on a position you already own, a 2B Reversal as a stop-out signal

How the 24 named plays map onto the four mechanical entry types the product actually tags trades with — PREV DAY HIGH BREAK, PREV LOW RECLAIM, RED TO GREEN, BASE BREAKOUT — a Flat Base Breakout IS a BASE BREAKOUT trigger; a Remount or U&R fires as PREV LOW RECLAIM; a Kicker Candle or Oops Reversal fires as RED TO GREEN

Why the three-tier split matters: 'when would I ever use this one' — a play misfiled as an entry gets traded too early, misfiled as an exit-read gets missed entirely when it should have gotten you out
Where the whole book lives in the product: Model Book → Setups, every one of the 24 with its glyph, one-line essence, and full playbook write-up

How the next four modules run, and the forced narrowing ahead: explore all four families in sim and replay first, but by the capstone you specialize into one or two — jumping between all 24 live is the single most-named reason traders fail
briefs.open_with: You just watched a stock break out of a base, add to it on a pullback, then start running parabolic — was that three different trades, or one trade with three different plays layered on top of it in sequence? If you can't answer that instantly, you don't have a playbook yet — you have a pattern-recognition party trick.
briefs.close_with: Takeaway: four families, three functions — primary, add-on, exit — one map, before a single setup gets taught in depth. Next up: 'The Breakout, End-to-End: Scan, Entry, Stop, and Position Sizing (Stair-Step Family)' — the Flat Base Breakout, taught to the tick, starting the deep dive into family one.

briefs.title: EP Pre-Market Homework: Float, Overhead Supply, Does the Gap Clear the Base — and the Season Clock
briefs.placement: UCT Foundations (Flagship Course), Module 8 — Setup Family III: Episodic Pivots and Catalyst Gaps, Lesson 2 of 4 (after 'The Episodic Pivot Defined: Qullamaggie's Breakout / EP / Parabolic Trio and Risk Rules', before 'Gap-Day Execution: The Tesla Breakaway-Gap Walkthrough and Oversize-Then-Trim Tactics')
talking_points: The three-question qualifying checklist before you touch ANY gap: float size, overhead supply, and does the gap clear the base — fail one, you don't take the trade
Float read: a thin float amplifies both the move and the whipsaw — size DOWN, not up, on small-float names, a rule that connects forward to Module 11's regime-adjusted sizing table

Overhead supply check: mark the last 6-12 months of price structure before the open — a gap running into a known resistance shelf 3-5% overhead is a materially different trade than one with clear air above

Does-the-gap-clear-the-base test, worked live on a real Episodic Pivot chart: the gap must clear the ENTIRE prior base structure, not just poke above it — a gap that closes back inside the base same day is a failed EP, not a pullback entry

Distinguishing catalyst quality with the same three-question checklist: an Episodic Pivot (10%+ surprise catalyst) vs. a Power Earnings Gap (blowout numbers specifically) vs. a Kicker Candle (prior-day-weak-then-gap-up trap) — same homework, different catalyst source
The repeatable routine: a five-minute pre-market pass — pull the gap list, run float, overhead, and base-clear on every name, keep only the ones that pass all three

State the season clock out loud: EP-family mastery takes three to four full earnings seasons of live reps — this is the slowest-mastery setup in the whole 24-play book, and pretending otherwise is how members blow up chasing gaps before they're ready
Worked side-by-side comparison: two gaps from the same morning, one clearing the checklist and one failing it — walk through exactly why only one gets touched
briefs.open_with: Every stock gapping 15% on this morning's scanner looks like the same trade. It isn't. Most of them fail this three-question checklist before you ever get to an entry price — and if you skip the homework, you're not trading Episodic Pivots, you're gambling on gaps.
briefs.close_with: Takeaway: float, overhead supply, does-the-gap-clear-the-base — three questions, five minutes, before any EP entry ever gets sized. And the honest clock is three to four earnings seasons before this setup should be sized like you trust it. Next up: 'Gap-Day Execution: The Tesla Breakaway-Gap Walkthrough and Oversize-Then-Trim Tactics' — how to actually get in, once a gap has passed homework.

briefs.title: Four-Family Placement Drill: 20 Mixed Charts, Name the Family First
briefs.placement: UCT Foundations (Flagship Course), Module 9 — Setup Family IV: Reversals, Reclaims, and the Short-Side Mirror, Lesson 5 of 5 (closing lesson of the module, after 'The Parabolic Short: Identification, Patience, and Sizing (Hardest Setup in the Book)')
talking_points: The drill format: 20 mixed charts pulled from all four families — Bases & Breakouts, Momentum & Trend, Gaps & Catalysts, Reversals & Reclaims — presented in random order, unlabeled
Guess-before-you-check, family-first: cover the setup name, look only at the chart's structure, and commit to one of the four families before revealing the answer — not the specific setup, the family

Why family-first beats setup-first: family recognition is the coarse skill that has to be automatic before the fine-grained setup name matters — a base mis-filed as a reversal gets traded with the wrong stop logic entirely
Worked example 1 on camera: a Flat Base Breakout, walked through the family tell — contraction, tightening pullbacks — before naming the specific setup
Worked example 2 on camera, the near-miss case: a chart that looks like a breakout but is actually a Failed H&S/Rounded Top reversal, and the one structural tell that separates them
Worked example 3 on camera, the other near-miss: an Episodic Pivot vs. a Kicker Candle — two gap setups that get confused, and the prior-day-close tell that distinguishes them
The rep count, stated exactly: 20 charts, one sitting, self-graded against the family rubric — not 'go practice recognizing setups' as a vague suggestion
This drill is the template for the platform's Chart Arcade mode: the same interleaved, family-first format becomes a permanent, gamified practice tool inside the product after this lesson ends
briefs.open_with: Cover the setup name on the next chart with your hand. If you can't tell me which of the four families it belongs to in under five seconds, you are not ready to trade any of the 24 plays live yet — you're pattern-matching on hope, not on a system.
briefs.close_with: Takeaway: family-first recognition, drilled interleaved rather than one family at a time, is the skill that makes the whole 24-play book usable under real time pressure. Next up: Module 10, Selling and Trade Management, starting with 'Selling Because You Were Wrong: The 12-Step Post-Entry Checklist' — you can now find and name every setup in the book; next you learn how to get out of one.

briefs.title: Regime-Adjusted Sizing: The GREEN/YELLOW/ORANGE × Setup-Grade Table
briefs.placement: UCT Foundations (Flagship Course), Module 11 — Progressive Exposure and Portfolio Command (Sizing, Second Pass), Lesson 2 of 4 (after 'Grade the Setup, Size the Risk: A/B/C Grading by Environment, Location, Familiarity, and Evidence', before 'Portfolio Heat and Correlation: Total Open Risk as One Number')
talking_points: The sizing formula restated at position level, verbatim: Account Risk % = Position Size % x Stop Distance % — every position's real risk is the product of these two numbers, never either one read alone
The universal ceiling underneath every regime adjustment: max 2% account risk per trade, and prefer under 1% — this floor never moves, no matter which cell of the table you're in
The table itself, stated exactly and put on screen: GREEN regime + A+ setup = 20-25% position size, YELLOW + A+ = 15%, ORANGE + A+ = 8%, and a B-grade setup inside ORANGE = skip entirely, no trade

Worked math across the table: take one real 8% stop distance and show how the identical position-size percentage produces a different account-risk percentage in each regime cell — the regime scales the position size, not the 2% ceiling itself

Why the table exists: this is the mechanical version of Module 3's exposure ladder — regime doesn't just gate whether you can open a NEW position, it gates exactly HOW BIG every position is allowed to be, cell by cell

The mechanical de-risk triggers that pull you OUT of a cell mid-trade: a regime downgrade from GREEN to YELLOW while a position is open, or the account drawdown triggers from Module 5 firing at minus-5% and minus-10%
Reading the live UCT Exposure Rating (0-150) against the table so it's never abstract: today's actual Exposure number tells you which regime cell you're sizing from, right now

Worked example, live: pull today's real regime plus a real A+ graded setup, size it correctly two different ways — once as if today were GREEN, once as if today were ORANGE — and show the dollar-risk difference on a fixed account size
briefs.open_with: Two members take the exact same A+ setup on the exact same day. One sizes it at 22% of the account. The other sizes it at 8%. Both of them are right — because they're trading it in two different market regimes, and if you don't know this table, you don't actually know how to size anything you trade.
briefs.close_with: Takeaway: GREEN+A+ = 20-25%, YELLOW+A+ = 15%, ORANGE+A+ = 8%, B-in-ORANGE = skip — memorize the table, then always verify it against today's actual UCT Exposure Rating before you size a single share. Next up: 'Portfolio Heat and Correlation: Total Open Risk as One Number' — now that one position is sized correctly, the next lesson caps what all of your positions can add up to at once.

briefs.title: Portfolio Heat and Correlation: Total Open Risk as One Number
briefs.placement: UCT Foundations (Flagship Course), Module 11 — Progressive Exposure and Portfolio Command (Sizing, Second Pass), Lesson 3 of 4 (after 'Regime-Adjusted Sizing: The GREEN/YELLOW/ORANGE × A/B/C Grade Table', before 'Beyond Fixed R:R: Expected Value and Context-Driven Size') Merges the dossier's "portfolio heat" and "correlation risk" bullets into one lesson.
talking_points: Define portfolio heat: sum every open position's account risk % (Account Risk % = Position Size % x Stop Distance %) into ONE number — five positions each risking 1.5% = 7.5% total heat, not five separate 1.5% bets.

The heat cap is regime-set, not trade-set: total portfolio heat must fit inside the regime-adjusted room, not just each position's individual room — GREEN+A+ can carry more open heat than YELLOW+A+ (15% max position) or ORANGE+A+ (8% max position); B-grade in ORANGE gets zero new heat (skip).

The "five positions = one trade" rule: when names share a sector, a catalyst window, a Theme Tracker bucket, or high beta to SPY/QQQ, their combined heat behaves like a single position's worth of risk — one headline can hit all five stops the same morning.
Practical correlation test: any TWO of (same sector, same earnings week, same theme bucket, high beta-to-index) = treat the group as correlated and count its heat as one line, not N lines.

Adds still cost heat: when a continuation setup (20 EMA Pullback, EMA Crossback) is an ADD to an existing winner, it draws from the SAME portfolio heat budget as a brand-new position — it is not free because the ticker is already in the book.

Worked example: build a 5-position book, sum the heat %, then identify which 3 names are correlated and show how a book that looks diversified on the position list reads as concentrated once heat is aggregated.

The cap tightens mechanically, not manually: as UCT Exposure and regime color downgrade, the allowable portfolio heat compresses automatically — this is the same lever as the position-size bands, applied at the book level.

Failure case: a trader disciplined at =2% per name still gets wiped by one gap-down because 6 of those names were all semiconductor names riding the same headline risk — heat, not per-trade sizing, was the actual blind spot.
briefs.open_with: A trader has 5 positions, each sized under 2% and individually textbook-disciplined — then one pre-market headline gaps all 5 down together because they're all semiconductor names. The loss reads like one blown-up trade, not five careful ones. Ask the room: how many trades do you actually have on right now?
briefs.close_with: Takeaway: portfolio heat is the one number that tells you whether you're actually diversified or secretly holding one oversized position split across five tickers, and the cap on that number moves with the regime automatically. Next lesson: "Beyond Fixed R:R: Expected Value and Context-Driven Size."

briefs.title: The Fixed-Field Journal and the Review Cadence — Inside Journal 2.0
briefs.placement: UCT Foundations (Flagship Course), Module 12 — The Inner Game and the Review Engine, Lesson 4 of 5 (after 'Trading as a Business: Building Your Plan and Weekly Review Routine', before 'A Real Monthly Review, Narrated End-to-End: Equity Curve, Setup Stats, and the Tilt-Recovery Story') Consolidates the dossier's fixed-field-journal, three-axis-grading, and review-cadence bullets into one product-native walkthrough inside Journal 2.0.
talking_points: The seven fixed fields, no free-form: physical state, timing, strategy anticipated, sourcing, entry quality, management, exit-vs-plan — plus an eighth artifact, the annotated screenshot, demonstrated live inside J2's own trade drawer.

Why fixed-field beats free-form: "I traded poorly" is not a fixable category; "no stop" or "chased entry" is — structure turns vague self-criticism into a named, countable failure mode you can track over time.

Three-axis grading — idea quality / execution / preparation, graded independently — and P&L is explicitly NOT one of the three axes: a well-executed A+ setup that still stops out grades well on execution even though it lost money.

The post-exit screenshot-tag-verdict protocol: every closed trade in J2 gets a chart screenshot, a setup tag pulled from the 24-setup library (Bull Flag, Flat Base Breakout, U&R, etc.), and a one-line verdict before it can leave "logged" status.

Daily tag to weekly to monthly rollup, automatic: the same seven fields aggregate inside J2's Analytics tab into setup-level win rate, average R, and process-score trend — the member re-enters nothing, the system computes it from the fixed schema.

Live demo: open a real closed trade in J2, walk the seven fields plus the three-axis grade plus the screenshot tag, then jump to the weekly review view and show that exact trade already rolled into setup-level stats.

The discipline this buys: a trader can be up money on a bad-process trade or down money on a good-process trade — the fixed schema is what separates outcome from decision instead of letting P&L do the grading.

Where this feeds forward: this is the exact data source Module 14's playbook and trade-plan defense will cite as evidence — the review engine is the raw material for the capstone artifact, not a separate habit.
briefs.open_with: Put a free-form entry on screen — "traded poorly today, forced a trade" — and ask what a coach could actually DO with that sentence. Nothing. Now show the same trade logged in J2's seven fields: strategy anticipated = none, entry quality = chased, sizing = oversized. Now it's fixable.
briefs.close_with: Takeaway: a trade isn't reviewed until it has seven fields, a three-axis grade, and a screenshot-tag-verdict — and this IS Journal 2.0, so today's practice trade is tomorrow's product fluency. Next lesson: "A Real Monthly Review, Narrated End-to-End: Equity Curve, Setup Stats, and the Tilt-Recovery Story" — the worked example that follows the schema you just learned.

briefs.title: Expressing a Swing With Calls: Strike, Expiry, and Delta Rules
briefs.placement: UCT Foundations (Flagship Course), Module 13 — The Options and Flow Overlay, Lesson 3 of 4 (after 'Flow as Confirmation, Never as Signal: Confluence With Your Setup', before 'Dealer Positioning and Gamma: Pins, Slingshots, and the Veto Hierarchy')
talking_points: When to sub calls for shares: the same setup, entry, and stop math still applies — calls only replace the equity leg when you specifically want a defined max risk equal to premium paid, not open-ended stop risk.

Strike selection rule: near-the-money to slightly ITM, delta roughly 0.60-0.75, so the option tracks the stock closely — avoid deep OTM strikes under 0.30 delta, which need a much bigger move just to keep pace with the chart's own stop-distance risk.

Expiry rule: buy at least 2-3x your expected holding period in calendar days — a 2-week swing gets a 4-6 week expiry minimum; never put a multi-week continuation setup into a weekly option, theta eats the thesis before it can play out.

Delta as a sizing proxy: a 0.70-delta contract behaves like roughly 70 shares — use that to reconcile options sizing back to the SAME Account Risk % = Position Size % x Stop Distance % formula so account risk still caps at 2%, prefer under 1%.

The defined-risk swap, stated plainly: max loss is the premium paid, not a wide equity stop — the reason to choose calls is a hard-capped downside on a setup whose equity stop would otherwise be uncomfortably wide (Parabolic Long, Episodic Pivot), not leverage for its own sake.
What to avoid: 0DTE or sub-2-week expiries on a swing setup — that's a day-trading instrument bolted onto a multi-week thesis, and theta decay outruns the pattern.
Worked example: take a live Bull Flag entry with a 2R target roughly 3 weeks out and select strike, delta, and expiry against the chart's actual entry/stop/target lines on screen.

Regime interaction: in ORANGE (8% position sizing), a defined-risk call often lets you stay engaged in an A+ setup without carrying the full equity-stop risk that regime would otherwise force you to shrink around.
briefs.open_with: A member bought weekly 0.15-delta calls on a 3-week Bull Flag because "calls are cheaper" — the setup played out exactly right and the calls still expired worthless from theta decay. Ask the room: which two numbers did they get wrong?
briefs.close_with: Takeaway: calls aren't a cheaper way to buy the same trade — they're a different risk instrument with their own strike, expiry, and delta rules, and every contract still has to resolve back to the 2% account-risk ceiling. Next lesson: "Dealer Positioning and Gamma: Pins, Slingshots, and the Veto Hierarchy" — where a chart/flow disagreement becomes the resolved veto case.

briefs.title: Dealer Positioning and Gamma: Pins, Slingshots, and the Veto Hierarchy
briefs.placement: UCT Foundations (Flagship Course), Module 13 — The Options and Flow Overlay, Lesson 4 of 4 (closing lesson of the module, after 'Expressing a Swing With Calls: Strike, Expiry, and Delta Rules') Merges the dossier's "dealer positioning and gamma context" bullet with the "veto hierarchy" bullet into one advanced-tier lesson, taught against UCT's live GEX surface.
talking_points: What dealer gamma exposure (GEX) measures: the net gamma dealers must hedge as price moves. Positive GEX = dealers sell rallies and buy dips, compressing range and "pinning" price toward a strike; negative GEX = dealers buy rallies and sell dips, amplifying moves and producing a "slingshot" through a level.

Reading UCT's live GEX surface: locate the zero-gamma flip level and the largest positive and negative gamma strikes — these behave as de facto support/resistance the same way a moving average does, but from dealer hedging flow, not price action.

Pin risk into expiration: heavy open interest at a strike plus positive GEX pulls price toward that strike into the close, especially monthly OpEx — this is why a stock can "refuse to move" right at a round-number strike on an otherwise clean chart.

Slingshot mechanics: when price breaks through a heavy negative-gamma zone, dealer hedging accelerates the move instead of dampening it — some breakouts run further and faster than the pattern alone would predict, and this is why.

The veto hierarchy, stated as a rule: the chart-defined entry and stop stay the trigger of record; gamma is a confirmation-or-caution overlay, never a standalone signal — heavy opposing gamma near your target means trim into it early, it does not cancel a qualified setup.

Veto case one: an A+ Flat Base Breakout sits just below a massive negative-gamma strike two dollars above pivot — the chart still says buy, but gamma says expect acceleration through that level rather than resistance, so target and trim logic adjust, not the entry.

Veto case two: heavy put buying or building dealer short-gamma against an otherwise clean long setup doesn't cancel the trade — it tightens the stop and lowers position size within the regime-adjusted band already in use.

Why this stays advanced-tier: gamma is a probabilistic overlay on a decision the chart has already qualified — misapplied, it becomes a discretionary excuse to override the mechanical rules from Module 5 (risk math) and Module 11 (sizing).
briefs.open_with: A member watching UCT's live GEX surface sees a stock pinned dead flat at $50 into Friday's OpEx despite a textbook Flat Base Breakout trigger three days earlier. Ask: is the setup broken, or is something holding price there that has nothing to do with the chart?
briefs.close_with: Takeaway: gamma explains why price behaves like it's on a leash near some strikes and shot out of a cannon past others — but it only ever adjusts trim, target, and size inside a trade the chart already qualified, it never replaces the chart's entry trigger. Next: Module 14 — Capstone: Build Your Playbook, starting with 'Define Your Layup: The One Setup You Execute Without Thinking.'

briefs.title: Write Your Playbook: The Five-Field Template for Your Two Setups
briefs.placement: UCT Foundations (Flagship Course), Module 14 — Capstone: Build Your Playbook, Lesson 3 of 5 (after 'The Case for One Setup: Depth Beats Breadth (Anand's Story)', before 'The Specialization Contract and Your One-Page Business Rules')
talking_points: The five fields, adapted from the SMB PlayBook template: Play Name, Fundamentals/Context, Technicals, Tape/Flow Read, Management — every finished entry has all five filled, not just the ones that felt natural to write.

Play Name convention: name it the way the firm names setups — specific and memorable ("Flat Base Breakout — Coiling Contraction Entry", not "breakout trade") — pulled straight from the Model Book setup catalog's own language.

Technicals must be numerically bounded, not descriptive: model it on the catalog's own standard — for Flat Base Breakout, each pullback smaller than the last, entry over the pivot high, riding the 9/20 EMA stack — never "buy when it looks tight."

Tape/Flow Read field: state in advance what unusual options activity or GEX context would CONFIRM this specific setup, tying directly back to Module 13 — written ahead of time, not improvised mid-trade.

Management field: entry trigger, initial structure-based stop (Module 5's rules), first partial level, trail rule, and which regime states this setup is even permitted in — e.g., skip a B-grade version of it in ORANGE.

Choosing your two setups: pull from the personality-fit data logged during the Module 6-9 family rotation drills — one flagship setup traded most confidently, one complementary setup from a different family.
Live example: fill all five fields on screen for one real setup (20 EMA Pullback) using an actual chart pulled from the member's own Journal 2.0 trade history, not a generic textbook chart.

What happens next: finished entries get mentor-annotated, and the strongest ones are promoted into the shared community playbook — review becomes content production, not a private notebook nobody else sees.
briefs.open_with: Put two "playbook entries" side by side — one is a paragraph vaguely describing a setup, the other is the five-field template filled with numbers pulled straight from a real J2 trade. Ask the room which one another trader could actually execute cold.
briefs.close_with: Takeaway: a playbook entry isn't finished until all five fields hold numbers you can defend, not adjectives you like the sound of. Next lesson: "The Specialization Contract and Your One-Page Business Rules."

briefs.title: The Trade-Plan Defense and the Graduation Gate
briefs.placement: UCT Foundations (Flagship Course), Module 14 — Capstone: Build Your Playbook, Lesson 5 of 5 (closing lesson of the module, after 'The Specialization Contract and Your One-Page Business Rules') This lesson IS the graduation gate — the flagship's terminal lesson.
talking_points: What gets defended: one full trade plan across four locked components — regime read, setup identification, position size, and exits — no component may be skipped or waved through.
The format this borrows: not multiple-choice recall, a presented decision defended against follow-up questions, CMT Level III-style, roughly 95% application-weighted rather than fact recall.

Regime component: state current UCT Exposure (0-150) and regime color, and the position size must match the regime-adjusted band unprompted — GREEN+A+ = 20-25%, YELLOW+A+ = 15%, ORANGE+A+ = 8%, B-grade in ORANGE = skip; get this wrong and the defense stops immediately.
Setup component: name the exact setup from the 24-play catalog, not "a breakout" — state its family and cite the numerically-bounded trigger criteria from that setup's Model Book entry.
Sizing component: show the arithmetic live on screen — Position Size % x Stop Distance % = Account Risk %, and it must clear the 2% ceiling, prefer under 1%, before the plan is accepted.

Exits component: stop price with the structural reason it sits there, the first partial level, and the timeframe-appropriate trail rule from Module 10 — a plan with no partial or trail rule fails automatically.
What "defend" means in practice: at least one adversarial follow-up per component ("what if the regime flips ORANGE mid-trade?") answered from the taught rules, not improvised on the spot.

The graduation gate itself: passing the defense — not watching every video, not calendar time — unlocks advanced-tier access, the same mastery-gate philosophy used at every checkpoint earlier in the course, now applied to the terminal artifact.
briefs.open_with: A member says, "I'm ready for advanced access, I finished every module." Ask them to defend one trade plan on the spot — regime, setup, size, exits — and watch exactly where it falls apart the first time someone pushes back on one number.
briefs.close_with: Takeaway: graduation isn't completion, it's a defended decision that survives one adversarial question per component — pass this and advanced-tier access unlocks. This is the flagship's terminal lesson — no next lesson follows within Module 14. From here the graduate moves into ongoing practice: the specialization track, monthly reviews (Module 12), and advanced-tier community access.

briefs.title: The Specialization Contract and Your One-Page Business Rules
briefs.placement: UCT Foundations (Flagship Course), Module 14 — Capstone: Build Your Playbook, Lesson 4 of 5 (after 'Write Your Playbook: The Five-Field Template for Your Two Setups', before 'The Trade-Plan Defense and the Graduation Gate')
talking_points: State the commitment on camera: name ONE setup from the 24-play book, inside ONE of the four families — Bases & Breakouts, Momentum & Trend, Gaps & Catalysts, Reversals & Reclaims — chosen from your own personality-fit data out of the sim rotation, not 'whatever sets up.'

The two numbers that make it a contract, not a New Year's resolution: a minimum of two full earnings seasons (~6 months) of live-market reps before you're allowed to grade your own edge on this setup, and a floor of 40 logged reps (paper + live, tagged to this one setup) before you're allowed to add a second.

Why those numbers aren't arbitrary: tie back to Module 8's earnings-season pacing lesson (episodic pivots take 3-4 seasons to trust) — pattern mastery is priced in market cycles, not calendar weeks, and this lesson says that out loud instead of implying it.

Reframe what the course owns vs. what the membership owns: the course taught the framework exactly once; Morning Wire, the Options Desk, Sunday Scans, and the live Desk sessions are where the 40 reps actually get logged — this is the moment the learner realizes the subscription IS the repetition engine, not a library they've already finished.

Build the sizing block of the one-page document live, field by field: write out the formula — 'Account Risk % = Position Size % x Stop Distance %' — then set a personal ceiling at or under 2%, with an explicit note that most of the room should be writing <1%, not the max.

Fill in the regime-adjusted sizing table on the same page: GREEN+A+ = 20-25% position, YELLOW+A+ = 15%, ORANGE+A+ = 8%, B-grade-in-ORANGE = skip — these are not reference numbers, they're the ones defended at the Graduation Gate.

Name the entry trigger on the page: which of PREV DAY HIGH BREAK / PREV LOW RECLAIM / RED TO GREEN / BASE BREAKOUT is the one this chosen setup actually fires on — a setup name without a named trigger is a preference, not a rule.

Close the loop to what's graded next: this page plus the defended trade plan are the two artifacts the Graduation Gate reviews — nothing on it can stay vague, because vague is exactly what gets sent back.
briefs.open_with: The mistake this lesson kills: finishing a swing-trading course and treating it as 'done' — then spending the next year hopping between all four families because nobody ever made you commit to a number. Open on camera with the direct question: 'You just defended one trade plan. Are you going to keep sampling all 24 plays, or pick one and give it two earnings seasons?' — force the commitment before you ever open the template.
briefs.close_with: Takeaway: walk away with a filled-in one-page rules document — one setup, two earnings seasons, 40 logged reps, your sizing math, your regime table, your entry trigger — not a saved file you never reopen. Next lesson: "The Trade-Plan Defense and the Graduation Gate" — where this page and your trade-plan defense get reviewed live before advanced-tier community access unlocks.

briefs.title: The Nightly Screen: From the Full Universe to a Tagged Watchlist
briefs.placement: UCT Intelligence Desk Video Library → Market Reading & the Daily Routine track → Scanning & the Daily Process module, Lesson 1 of 6 (opening lesson; replaces video id 75, "The Process of Scanning Stocks and Building a Watchlist" — zero transcript, no AI chapters, generic boilerplate description; before 'Seven Custom Scans: Building the Morning Watchlist').
talking_points: Regime check first, always: read the UCT Exposure reading (0-150 scale) and the current regime phase before opening a single chart — a hostile/ORANGE tape changes what you're even looking for tonight, not just how much you're allowed to risk.

Start from the full tradable universe, not your memory: the raw pool is the entire cap universe, not the five names your group chat is hyping — the discipline is running the same filter every session, not chasing tickers you already have an opinion on.
Run the three mechanical scans, in order: Pullback MA (up to 30 candidates), Remount (up to 10), Gappers/News (up to 10) — three different STAGES of setup readiness, not three competing strategies.
The hard gate before any candidate earns a second look: average daily range has to clear roughly 4% — anything tighter gets filtered before you waste a look on the chart.

Score what survives on three tells: how close price is kissing the rising 20 EMA, how tight the last several bars are closing, and whether volume is drying up into the move — the difference between 'watch' and 'skip.'

Tag every survivor by family and trigger, not just symbol: which of the four setup families it belongs to — Bases & Breakouts, Momentum & Trend, Gaps & Catalysts, Reversals & Reclaims — and which entry type it's setting up for: PREV DAY HIGH BREAK, PREV LOW RECLAIM, RED TO GREEN, or BASE BREAKOUT. An untagged ticker on a list isn't a watchlist entry.

Log the session on a fixed-field Nightly Screen Worksheet — regime reading, scan counts, ADR-cleared names, family/entry tags — the same fields every night, so twenty nights becomes reviewable data instead of twenty forgotten browser tabs.

The count is not the target: some nights the filter returns three clean names, some nights zero — grade the process (did you run the same filter tonight), never the number of survivors; nothing on the list is a trade yet, only a tagged candidate still waiting on size and trigger confirmation.
briefs.open_with: The mistake this lesson kills: opening twenty browser tabs of stocks your group chat is hyping and calling that a 'watchlist' with no repeatable filter behind it. Open on a real screen recording of a chaotic ad-hoc list, then ask on camera: 'If the tape flipped ORANGE tonight, would half of these names even survive your own rules?' — that's the gap a mechanical nightly screen closes.
briefs.close_with: Takeaway: a repeatable four-step filter — regime check, three mechanical scans, the ADR/tightness/volume gate, and family-plus-entry-type tagging — that turns the full universe into a short, labeled list every single night, regardless of how many names survive. Next: 'ETF-First Scanning: Surface Stocks Before They Run' — now that you have a screened watchlist, catch the relative-strength moves an ETF surfaces before they're obvious on the single-name chart.
